query: Consider the following context: The recent trend of high-entropy alloys (HEAs) was studied extensively for their promising mechanical properties, but individual constituents' effects have remained unexplored. In that context, which method can be used for the effects of changing the percentage of elements of HfNbTaTiZr-HEA on the mechanical properties, and why?

generation.hypothesis: If we systematically vary the ratio of each element in HfNbTaTiZr using arc melting, then mechanical properties (e.g., strength, hardness) will increase for higher fractions of heavier elements like Hf or Zr, with possible trade-offs in ductility due to increased lattice distortion.
generation.material_initial_state: Equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr high-entropy alloy manufactured via arc melting
generation.intervention: Change atomic fractions of Hf, Nb, Ta, Ti, and Zr systematically using arc melting, then conduct standard mechanical tests (e.g., hardness, tension, or compression)
generation.conditions: Alloys synthesized via vacuum arc melting under comparable processing parameters, followed by standard homogenization and testing at room temperature
generation.structural_mediator: Single-phase BCC matrix with lattice distortion influenced by heavier elements
generation.mechanism: Heavier atoms (Hf, Zr) impart greater lattice distortion, altering dislocation motion to affect mechanical strength and ductility
generation.predicted_outcome: Shifting composition toward heavier elements will incrementally increase strength and hardness, with some reduction in ductility; the exact magnitude of change is not yet established
generation.baseline: Equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr produced and tested under the same conditions
generation.boundary: Results may differ if non-equilibrium processing routes or extreme compositions disrupt single-phase BCC formation
generation.uncertainty: Quantitative changes in performance for each compositional shift remain undetermined without direct experimentation

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare multiple HfNbTaTiZr alloys with systematic compositional variations via arc melting. Keep melting and cooling conditions consistent. Perform mechanical tests (hardness, tensile, or compression), microstructural characterization (SEM/TEM), and phase analysis (XRD).
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If increasing the fraction of heavier elements does not produce the hypothesized rise in strength or if ductility remains unchanged at higher heavy-element content, the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Abstract High entropy alloys (HEA) have been one of the most attractive groups of materials for researchers in the last several years. Since HEAs are potential candidates for many (e.g., refractory, cryogenic, medical) applications, their properties are studied intensively. The most frequent method of HEA synthesis is arc or induction melting. Powder metallurgy is a perspective technique of alloy synthesis and therefore in this work the possibilities of synthesis of HfNbTaTiZr HEA from powders were studied. Blended elemental powders were sintered, hot isostatically pressed, and subsequently swaged using a special technique of swaging where the sample is enveloped by a titanium alloy. This method does not result in a full density alloy due to cracking during swaging. Spark plasma sintering (SPS) of mechanically alloyed powders resulted in a fully dense but brittle specimen. The most promising result was obtained by SPS treatment of gas atomized powder with low oxygen content. The microstructure of HfNbTaTiZr specimen prepared this way can be refined by high pressure torsion deformation resulting in a high hardness of 410 HV10 and very fine microstructure with grain size well below 5
